claim: The ISS safety requirements treat the US airlock as a higher-oxygen location than the rest of the station (worst case 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia versus 24.1% at 14.7 psia elsewhere), and say end items that will operate in the airlock during EVA preparations should be tested or evaluated in that airlock environment.
quote: The worst-case oxygen environment for ISS is 14.7 psia with 24.1-percent oxygen for all locations except the USOS airlock. The airlock worst-case environment is 10.2 psia with 30-percent oxygen. End items materials should be tested or evaluated in the worst-case airlock environment if they intend to operate in the airlock during EVA preparations.
source_title: ISS Safety Requirements Documents: International Space Station Program (Baseline), SSP 51721
source_authors: Jenny R. Andrews, Monica Ann Garcia, Patrick Leo Mitchell, Sally Kay Nash Vail (NASA Johnson Space Center and contractors), for the NASA International Space Station Program
locator: Section 4.7.1.1 Flammable Materials, Rationale, p. 4-78 (repeated in Appendix D.4.7.1.1, p. D-53)

conditions.pressure_text: Airlock worst case 10.2 psia with 30-percent oxygen; all other ISS locations worst case 14.7 psia with 24.1-percent oxygen

limits: These are worst-case design environments used to evaluate materials (maximum allowed, not the typical composition), not measured fire outcomes. The text names no specific material or item. It does not say how a battery-powered instrument behaves in the airlock, only that items intended to operate there should be evaluated in that environment.
usefulness: (b)(c) Gives the first zone type with numbers: the airlock during EVA preparation is a documented elevated-oxygen location (30% at 10.2 psia) where a cargo item that passed at ISS cabin conditions needs its own evaluation.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact. Context read: Section 4.7.1.1 Rationale, p. 4-78 (footer), repeated in Appendix D.4.7.1.1, p. D-53 (footer). Claim matches the quote (USOS airlock 10.2 psia / 30%; all other ISS locations 14.7 psia / 24.1%; test or evaluate in airlock environment if intending to operate in the airlock during EVA preparations). Metadata normalised to the NTRS record 20210009936 (public, 2019-09).

claim: NASA's flammability handbook says hardware designed for ISS is acceptable for transport in pressurized areas of vehicles with higher oxygen concentrations provided it is unpowered and stowed in a locker or validated fire barrier stowage bag (unpowered metal boxes, which may be painted, are also acceptable).
quote: Hardware designed for internal or external use on ISS is acceptable for transport in pressurized areas of vehicles with higher oxygen concentrations, provided it is unpowered and stowed in a locker or validated fire barrier stowage bag. Unpowered metal boxes, which may be painted, are also acceptable.
source_title: Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, JSC 29353D (December 2024)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: Section 5.4, note under key factor (a) Oxygen concentration, p. 16

conditions.pressure_text: 'vehicles with higher oxygen concentrations' than ISS; no value given in this sentence (Table 1 of the handbook lists 24.1% at 14.5 psia ISS internal, 30% at 10.2 psia airlock, 36-40% at 8.2 psia lunar or Martian surface habitable elements)

limits: A transport allowance ('acceptable for transport'), not a rule for use or operation at the destination. It does not say what happens to hardware outside the allowance except in the next sentence (assess it for flammability at the higher oxygen concentration and pressure). Reading a battery-powered instrument as outside the allowance is an inference. The handbook does not define 'unpowered' for a switched-off device that still holds a charged battery (nearby text speaks of containers with 'internal sources of power'), so the item's status needs the safety review to decide.
usefulness: (a)(b) Core of the demo story: an ISS-qualified, battery-powered item moving to a higher-oxygen destination loses the simple 'ISS-approved' pass and has to be stowed or re-assessed.
verifier_note: Original claim said 'only if ... locker or fire-barrier stowage bag'. The source says 'provided it is unpowered and stowed in a locker or validated fire barrier stowage bag' and, in the next sentence, that 'Unpowered metal boxes, which may be painted, are also acceptable'; the assess-otherwise rule is a separate sentence. Claim reworded to 'provided' and the metal-box alternative added; quote extended by that sentence (47 words, found exact). Section 5.4 key factor (a), printed p. 16 confirmed by page footer. Table 1 values in the conditions text checked against Table 1 (pp. 11-12): ISS internal 24.1% at 14.5 psia, ISS airlock 30% at 10.2 psia, lunar or Martian surface habitable elements 36-40% at 8.2 psia (footnote: 33.7% minimum).

quote: provided it is unpowered and stowed in a locker or validated fire barrier stowage bag. Unpowered metal boxes, which may be painted, are also acceptable. Assess hardware not meeting these constraints for flammability at the higher oxygen concentration and pressure.

conditions.pressure_text: 'the higher oxygen concentration and pressure' of the receiving vehicle; no value in this sentence

usefulness: (a) States the action that applies to a powered item: re-assess at the destination's oxygen and pressure rather than carry over the ISS result.

claim: A material that is acceptable at 24.1% oxygen may already be flammable at 24.5% oxygen at the same pressure, because small increases in oxygen concentration can change the flammability rating.
quote: Since even small increases in oxygen concentration can change the flammability rating, a material that is acceptable in 24.1 percent oxygen may be flammable in 24.5 percent oxygen at the same pressure.
source_title: Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, JSC 29353D (December 2024)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: Section 5.4, key factor (a) Oxygen concentration, p. 16

conditions.pressure_text: 'the same pressure' (not numerically stated in this sentence); 24.1 percent is the ISS maximum at 14.7 psia per the same handbook

limits: A generic statement about how sharply ratings can change; no material or thickness is named and 'may be flammable' is not a test result. Ratings depend on material thickness, test configuration and substrate, so it cannot be applied to a specific material without its own test data. The handbook gives the ISS 24.1% maximum at 14.7 psia in its Section 5.1 text and at 14.5 psia in Table 1.
usefulness: (a)(c) Shows that the oxygen step from ISS cabin air to a destination atmosphere can flip a material from acceptable to flammable even with a small increase.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, Section 5.4 key factor (a), p. 16. Claim matches. Only the limits text was corrected: the handbook gives the ISS maximum as 24.1% at 14.7 psia in its Section 5.1 text but 24.1% at 14.5 psia in Table 1, so the limits no longer cite a single pressure. The quoted sentence is a general statement ('may be flammable'), not a result for a named material.

claim: A topical white paper by fire researchers at USRA/NASA Glenn and partner institutions says material flammability limits are not expected to meet current requirements under the elevated oxygen (34%) and reduced pressure (8.2 psi) planned for future lunar habitats, and that these conditions are also expected to affect fire emissions.
quote: material flammability limits are not expected to meet current requirements under elevated O2 (34%) and reduced pressure conditions (8.2 psi) planned for future lunar habitats; these conditions are also expected to effect fire emissions.
source_title: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (white paper for the NASEM Decadal Survey on Biological and Physical Sciences Research in Space)
source_authors: Claire Fortenberry (USRA, NASA Glenn), Xiaoliang Wang (Desert Research Institute), Thomas Cleary (NIST), John Easton (Case Western Reserve University, NASA Glenn), Gordon Berger (USRA, NASA Glenn), Marit Meyer (NASA Glenn)
locator: Introduction, p. 2

conditions.gravity: lunar habitat (partial gravity), not specified in this sentence

limits: An expectation stated in a white paper, not a test result. 'Current requirements' refers to existing spacecraft flammability requirements; no material is named and no gravity level is stated. JSC 29353D Table 1 lists a 36-40% maximum oxygen concentration at 8.2 psia for habitable exploration elements on the lunar or Martian surface, with 33.7% as the minimum (its footnote 4), so 34% is a planned value in this paper, not a measured one.
usefulness: (a)(c) Directly supports the destination side of the demo: oxygen about 34% at 8.2 psi is where materials accepted on ISS are expected to fall short.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, p. 2 confirmed in the PDF (page 4 also states 'planned environment for future lunar habitats is 34% O2 and 8.2 psi'). Attribution corrected: this is a white paper submitted to the National Academies by authors at USRA/NASA Glenn, Desert Research Institute, NIST and Case Western Reserve University, not a NASA-only statement; claim restated as 'not expected to meet' and 'expected to affect'. Limits extended with JSC 29353D Table 1 (36-40% maximum at 8.2 psia, 33.7% minimum in footnote 4).

claim: In the Apollo 204 Review Board's spacecraft boilerplate (mockup) tests, the rate of flame propagation, the rate of pressure increase, the maximum pressures and the extent of conflagration in a 5 psia oxygen atmosphere were much less severe than in a 16.5 psia oxygen atmosphere.
quote: The rate of flame propagation, the rate of pressure increase and the maximum pressures achieved and the extent of conflagration in 5 psia oxygen boilerplate tests was much less severe than observed in the 16.5 psia oxygen boilerplate tests.
source_title: Report of Apollo 204 Review Board, Appendix D-8: Report of Panel 8, Materials Review
source_authors: Apollo 204 Review Board, Panel 8 (Materials Review)
locator: Appendix D-8 (Report of Panel 8), special investigations, fire propagation, 'Correlation of C/M mockup tests', p. D-8-33

conditions.pressure_text: oxygen atmosphere at 5 psia versus 16.5 psia (oxygen percentage not stated in this passage)

limits: 1967 ground tests on a mockup of the Apollo spacecraft 012 with its own materials (nylon netting, Velcro, foam). Not a lunar-habitat result and not for modern materials. The same finding says burning or charring was limited to approximately 29 percent of the nonmetallic materials by oxygen depletion, and the report's determination that the fire would be far less severe and slower at 5 psia holds only if additional large quantities of oxygen are not fed into the fire, so the contrast is not a pressure effect alone. The report also finds that a fire at 5 psia oxygen 'could be fatal', so lower pressure reduces severity but does not remove the hazard.
usefulness: (c) Historic evidence that, in an oxygen atmosphere with the same fuel, 5 psia gave a much slower and less intense fire than 16.5 psia (partly because oxygen was used up). It shows pressure matters, not a threshold for any modern material.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact. Page D-8-33 confirmed in the PDF (PDF page 219). Source wording is 'boilerplate tests' (the section heading is 'Correlation of C/M mockup tests'); claim now uses the source's terms and lists all four quantities in the quote. Limits corrected: the same FINDING says burning or charring was 'limited to approximately 29 percent of the nonmetallic materials by oxygen depletion', and the DETERMINATION that the fire would be 'far less severe and slower' at 5 psia is conditional on no additional large quantities of oxygen being fed into the fire, so the difference is not a pressure effect alone. The report also says a 5 psia oxygen fire 'could be fatal'.

claim: On Mir in February 1997 a solid-fuel oxygen generator canister ignited, shot a three-foot flame with sparks and molten metal across the Kvant-1 module, produced dense smoke, and the flame blocked the route to one of the Soyuz escape vehicles.
quote: the canister ignited, shooting a three-foot flame with sparks and bits of molten metal across the module and generating a large quantity of dense smoke. The flame blocked the evacuation route to the Soyuz spacecraft docked at the aft end of Kvant-1, the vehicle Korzun, Kaleri, and Ewald would use in an emergency evacuation.
source_title: 25 Years Ago: Fire Aboard Space Station Mir
source_authors: John Uri, NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: NASA History article, paragraph beginning 'Shortly after dinner on Feb. 24'
limits: A historical incident narrative on a Russian oxygen-generating device, not a cargo item. The article reports the likely cause as hydrocarbon (latex glove) contamination of the canister. It shows an oxygen source as a fire source and a fire blocking egress, not a general rule for stowing instruments.
usefulness: (b) Concrete example of an oxygen-source location becoming a fire location and of a hazard placed next to an evacuation route.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact (single occurrence). Article opened: NASA History, John Uri (Johnson Space Center), published 23 Feb 2022; text says the flame 'cut off access to one of the two Soyuz escape vehicles' and gives the likely cause as latex working glove material introduced into the canister (after two years of study). Claim matches the quote. Usefulness stays an inference about placement; the article does not discuss cargo stowage.

claim: On spacecraft, ventilation fans replace natural convection and can supply the air a fire needs, so a fire can spread in any direction rather than only upward.
quote: Ventilation fans on space vehicles replace natural convection and can supply the air a fire needs to burn. Under these circumstances, the fire can spread in any direction, rather than just upward.
source_title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-008: Fire Protection (Rev A, 11/29/2023)
source_authors: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO)
locator: Overview, p. 2
limits: Qualitative summary in an OCHMO technical brief 'for reference only'; it does not give a flow speed, and it does not say how flow changes burning in partial gravity.
usefulness: (b)(c) Backs the 'near ventilation flow' zone: a vent outlet or fan path is where a small fire gets oxygen and can spread.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, p. 2 confirmed by PDF page. Claim matches. The brief is 'derived from NASA-STD-3001 and is for reference only'; the statement is qualitative.

claim: JSC 29353D says that in NASA airflow tests of a vented sheet-metal electronics box (polyurethane foam, circuit boards and polyalkene-insulated wire inside), the box was an effective fire container at flows below 10 scfm and above 20 scfm, but not at flows between those values.
quote: At velocities below 10 scfm and above 20 scfm, the box is an effective fire container. At velocities between these values, it is not.
source_title: Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, JSC 29353D (December 2024)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: Section 9.5 Vented Containers (airflow tests, TR-325-001 and TR-325-002, 1984), printed p. 38 (test set-up on p. 37)

conditions.flow_text: 6.5 to 20.0 scfm (volumetric flow through the box, not a velocity); fire escaped the box in one test at 15 scfm; contained at 10 scfm and below and at 20 scfm and above

converted_values: 10 scfm = 4.7 L/s; 20 scfm = 9.4 L/s (standard cubic feet per minute); 10.0 psia = 68.9 kPa
limits: One box design and one set of materials with standard igniters. scfm is volumetric flow through the box, not cabin air velocity, so no speed follows. The source gives 30% oxygen at 10.0 psia and 6.5 to 20.0 scfm for 'these tests' and does not restate conditions for the additional tests at lower and higher flows. In the main tests the fire was contained in every case except one at 15 scfm, where the burning foam ignited a 6-in diameter aluminum vent screen of window-screen material (about 300 mesh); the handbook notes that finer 60-mesh aluminum is more effective. Gravity level is not stated and the reports are dated 1984, so this is not a microgravity or lunar-gravity result. The handbook itself calls generalising flow effects on vented containers difficult and says the worst-case flow depends on configuration and may be affected by gravity and pressure.
usefulness: (c) Measured flow dependence in a handbook example: a mid-range flow was the worst case and the box contained the fire at low and at high flow. It shows why 'near a ventilation path' is not simply safe or unsafe.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, printed p. 38 confirmed by page footer (Section 9.5, tests cited as TR-325-001 and TR-325-002, 1984). Claim narrowed to what the quote says; the 15 scfm breach, the 30% O2 / 10.0 psia and the 6.5-20.0 scfm range come from the surrounding paragraph and are kept as conditions and limits, not as claim text. The source states that 30% O2 at 10.0 psia and 6.5 to 20.0 scfm apply to 'these tests'; the additional tests at lower and higher flows are described without conditions, so those conditions are marked as such. 'Window screen' vent detail added from the same paragraph: the one breach burned through a 6-in diameter aluminum vent screen of window screen material (about 300 mesh), whereas the handbook says 60-mesh aluminum screen performs better. Flow is volumetric (scfm), not a speed.

quote: Small, low-voltage alkaline and coin batteries are still believed to be incapable of delivering powers required for ignition, although larger batteries (such as lithium-ion rechargeable batteries for portable electronic devices) can certainly achieve higher power levels.

source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center

limits: Qualitative: no wattage threshold is given for lithium-ion batteries, and the handbook says the power threshold is under re-evaluation. It does not say that a given instrument battery will ignite anything. Section 5.6 (p. 18) of the same handbook says lithium-ion battery lots verified to meet the JSC 20793 spacecraft battery requirements are considered to be improbable ignition sources in flammability configuration analysis, and that this does not remove the need for extinguishment equipment able to control lithium-ion fires.
usefulness: (a)(c) Separates the item's lithium-ion battery from the benign small-battery case: larger lithium-ion batteries can reach higher power than the small alkaline and coin cells that are believed not to ignite solids. Whether a certified battery counts as an ignition source in the analysis is governed by Section 5.6 (improbable if verified to JSC 20793).
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, Section 5.2, printed p. 13 confirmed. Claim matches. Limits and usefulness corrected for balance: Section 5.6 (p. 18) of the same handbook says lithium-ion battery lots verified to the JSC 20793 spacecraft battery requirements are considered improbable ignition sources in flammability configuration analysis, while emergency extinguishment equipment must still be able to control lithium-ion fires. The original usefulness text ('not automatically exempt') presented only one side.

claim: The ISS fire response includes manually removing electrical power from hardware in the affected module, which should cease any continuous ignition sources.
quote: Manually remove electrical power: Removing electrical power from hardware within the affected module should cease any continuous ignition sources
source_title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-008: Fire Protection (Rev A, 11/29/2023)
source_authors: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO)
locator: ISS Fire Safety Strategy, step 4, p. 3
limits: Published response strategy, not a verified current crew checklist. It does not show that removing module power stops an item that carries its own battery; the brief says nothing about portable battery-powered cargo.
usefulness: (b) Shows the published ISS response treats powered hardware as a continuing ignition source to be de-powered. The brief does not discuss portable battery-powered items; whether module power-down reaches such an item is an inference to confirm elsewhere.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, step 4 of the ISS Fire Safety Strategy, p. 3 confirmed by PDF page. Claim matches. Usefulness text rewritten: the brief does not discuss items with their own batteries, so that link is an inference.

claim: A white paper by fire researchers at USRA/NASA Glenn and partner institutions states that laptop lithium-ion battery fires constitute one of the most likely and most dangerous spacecraft fire scenarios threatening crew safety in long-duration missions.
quote: In particular, laptop LIB fires constitute one of the most likely and most dangerous spacecraft fire scenarios threatening crew safety in long-duration missions.
source_title: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (white paper for the NASEM Decadal Survey on Biological and Physical Sciences Research in Space)
source_authors: Claire Fortenberry (USRA, NASA Glenn), Xiaoliang Wang (Desert Research Institute), Thomas Cleary (NIST), John Easton (Case Western Reserve University, NASA Glenn), Gordon Berger (USRA, NASA Glenn), Marit Meyer (NASA Glenn)
locator: Research Topics and Challenges, A, p. 3
limits: A judgement in a white paper (cites its own reference 10), not a measured probability. It concerns laptop packs, not a specific battery-powered instrument.
usefulness: (c) NASA-authored ranking that puts portable lithium-ion devices among the most credible spacecraft fire sources.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, p. 3 confirmed in the PDF. Claim text matches. Attribution corrected: a white paper to the National Academies decadal survey by authors at USRA/NASA Glenn, Desert Research Institute, NIST and Case Western Reserve University, not a NASA position.

claim: NASA's handbook says flammable items in fully enclosed lockers or fire-barrier bags are not a fire risk while unpowered, but powered payloads stowed in lockers for a whole mission, or placed where a locker would be, need a flammability evaluation because they present a potential fire hazard.
quote: Flammable materials stowed in these containers do not constitute a fire risk while in the containers, provided they are unpowered. Evaluate powered payloads/experiments stowed in lockers for an entire mission or located in place of a locker from a flammability standpoint because they present a potential fire hazard.
source_title: Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, JSC 29353D (December 2024)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: Section 6.3 Intermediate Containers, p. 20

conditions.pressure_text: not stated in the quoted sentences (the next sentence of the section addresses atmospheres containing up to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia for commercial electronics stowage constraints)
conditions.flow_text: intermediate containers have no active vents or airflow

limits: Concerns powered payloads stowed for an entire mission or located in place of a locker; it says nothing about how long a short stowage counts or about charging. It applies to NASA-provided fully enclosed stowage lockers and validated fire barrier stowage bags; the same section says the MPCV stowage lockers are not fully enclosed (open grid inner walls), refers to issues with current cargo transfer bag designs (Section 5.3) and says the ISS Zero-G Softracks may have similar issues. The handbook says it does not consider partial-gravity effects.
usefulness: (b) Says closed stowage is safe for unpowered fuel but not for powered items, which is the case for a battery-powered instrument stowed in a locker.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, Section 6.3, printed p. 20 confirmed by page footer. Claim matches. Conditions and limits corrected: the sentence about 'atmospheres containing up to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia' that follows in the source concerns stowage constraints for commercial electronics, not the quoted lockers sentence; and the same section warns about current cargo transfer bag designs and that MPCV lockers are not fully enclosed.

claim: The ISS safety requirements document says the rack interface requirements document (IRD) addresses the use of Warning alerts for subrack fire detection via parameter monitoring when the subrack volume does not exchange air with the rack smoke detector.
quote: The IRD addresses the use of Warning alerts for subrack fire detection via parameter monitoring when the subrack volume does not exchange air with the rack smoke detector.
source_title: ISS Safety Requirements Documents: International Space Station Program (Baseline), SSP 51721
source_authors: Jenny R. Andrews, Monica Ann Garcia, Patrick Leo Mitchell, Sally Kay Nash Vail (NASA Johnson Space Center and contractors), for the NASA International Space Station Program
locator: Appendix D.4.5.2.1 RTM - ISS Caution and Warning System, p. D-50

conditions.flow_text: no air exchange between the subrack volume and the rack smoke detector

limits: Describes how the requirements document refers to the case, not how long detection takes. The quote says only that the IRD addresses parameter monitoring with Warning alerts for such subracks; it does not describe the monitoring or state that smoke detection is excluded. It refers to ISS racks and subracks, not to a cargo bag or a locker in the cabin, so applying it to cargo stowage is an analogy.
usefulness: (b) Shows ISS requirements treat a volume that does not exchange air with a smoke detector as a special case that needs parameter monitoring; applying it to cargo stowage is an analogy.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, p. D-50 confirmed. Original claim said requirements handle the case 'instead of smoke detection'; the quote only says the IRD (interface requirements document) addresses Warning alerts for subrack fire detection via parameter monitoring when the subrack volume does not exchange air with the rack smoke detector. Claim narrowed to that wording. Metadata normalised to the NTRS record.

claim: In space smoke does not rise, so spacecraft smoke detectors are placed within the ventilation system rather than on ceilings.
quote: On Earth, smoke detectors are installed on the ceiling or upper section of a wall because that's the direction in which smoke travels. In space, smoke doesn't rise, so detectors are placed within the ventilation system.
source_title: NASA-STD-3001 Technical Brief OCHMO-TB-008: Fire Protection (Rev A, 11/29/2023)
source_authors: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO)
locator: Overview, p. 2

conditions.flow_text: detectors sit in the ventilation system; no speed given

limits: General statement; it does not say how long smoke from a hidden or stagnant location takes to reach a detector, and it does not describe lunar gravity behaviour.
usefulness: (b) Background for why smoke from a hidden or closed volume may reach a detector late: a detector in the ventilation system sees smoke the airflow carries to it (an inference; the brief does not state a delay).
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, p. 2 confirmed by PDF page. Claim matches. Usefulness ('hidden or closed stowage is detected late') is an inference from the quote, not a stated result.

claim: NASA's crew-health standard rationale says automated fire systems are to be used where crew cannot extinguish fires, including fires when crew could be absent and fires in volumes inaccessible to the crew.
quote: Automated systems are to be used where crews are not capable of extinguishing fires (large fires or fires where crew could be absent, or fires in volumes inaccessible to the crew).
source_title: NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2, section 9.8.2.1 Fire Detecting, Warning, and Extinguishing [V2 9059] (web edition, rationale text)
source_authors: NASA Office of the Chief Health and Medical Officer (OCHMO)
locator: Section 9.8.2.1 [V2 9059] Fire Detecting, Warning, and Extinguishing, Rationale
limits: A design rationale for vehicle fire-protection systems, not a rule about cargo stowage and not a test. The web edition text carries no revision date; the page lists a Volume 2 PDF dated Jul 15, 2026 and OCHMO-TB-008 cites NASA-STD-3001 Volume 2 Rev D, so which revision this web text reflects is not established.
usefulness: (b) Backs 'closed or inaccessible volume' as a recognized special case where the crew cannot respond by hand.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact (single occurrence), Section 9.8.2.1 [V2 9059] rationale text on the NASA web edition. Claim matches. Limits corrected: the web page lists a Volume 2 PDF dated Jul 15, 2026 and OCHMO-TB-008 cites Volume 2 Rev D, while the web text itself carries no revision date, so source_year is left null.

claim: A white paper by fire researchers at USRA/NASA Glenn and partner institutions states that during the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME) the ISS detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of the tests.
quote: the ISS detector failed to alarm for Kapton smoke in half of the tests and for Teflon smoke in two-thirds of the tests
source_title: Research Questions and Challenges for Improved Spacecraft Fire Detection (white paper for the NASEM Decadal Survey on Biological and Physical Sciences Research in Space)
source_authors: Claire Fortenberry (USRA, NASA Glenn), Xiaoliang Wang (Desert Research Institute), Thomas Cleary (NIST), John Easton (Case Western Reserve University, NASA Glenn), Gordon Berger (USRA, NASA Glenn), Marit Meyer (NASA Glenn)
locator: Introduction, p. 2

conditions.gravity: microgravity (the paper describes SAME as the first study of oxidative pyrolysis particles in microgravity)

limits: A summary in a white paper of the SAME tests (references 3 to 5 there), not the primary SAME report. It covers smoke from overheated Kapton and Teflon, common insulation, not smoke from a battery failure.
usefulness: (a)(b) Shows the ISS detector can miss smoke from common electrical insulation, so a small hidden fire in electronics can go undetected longer.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact, p. 2 confirmed in the PDF. Claim narrowed to the white paper's wording: it says 'During the Smoke Aerosol Measurement Experiment (SAME), ... the ISS detector failed to alarm'; it does not call SAME a NASA experiment and does not state where the smoke tests were run (the claim's 'NASA's' was removed; gravity field reworded to 'microgravity' as stated). Attribution corrected to the white-paper authors.

claim: JSC 29353D says stowage bags can have flammable items stowed inside provided they do not contain ignition sources (such as electrical power) and are not susceptible to spontaneous ignition or chemical reaction, and that the ISS and MPCV Programs allow fully certified and undamaged batteries, including lithium-ion rechargeable batteries, to be stowed inside such bags without additional containment.
quote: Stowage bags can have flammable items stowed inside provided they do not contain ignition sources (such as electrical power) and are not susceptible to spontaneous ignition or chemical reaction. The ISS and MPCV Programs allow fully certified and undamaged batteries, including lithium-ion rechargeable batteries, to be stowed inside such bags without additional containment.
source_title: Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, JSC 29353D (December 2024)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: Section 8.6 Stowage Bags and Lockers, p. 29

conditions.pressure_text: Nomex bag acreage verified in up to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia (same section); the quoted sentences state no atmosphere

limits: An allowance for the ISS and MPCV programs for certified, undamaged batteries; it does not cover charging or higher-oxygen lunar habitats. The same section says the acceptability of the ISS and MPCV cargo transfer bags is currently uncertain (in recent HLS large-scale testing the bags propagated fire through burning seams, hook-and-loop fasteners and plastic zippers, Section 5.3, p. 14), that bag acreage was verified only up to 30% oxygen at 10.2 psia, and that no Nomex material meets flammability requirements for HLS environments containing >36 percent oxygen (p. 28) and Nomex is flammable in exploration environments containing 36 percent oxygen and above (p. 29).
usefulness: (b) Concrete stowage rule for a certified lithium-ion battery in a fire-barrier bag and the condition that the bag has no live power.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact (53 words), Section 8.6, printed p. 29 confirmed by page footer. 'Fire-barrier' removed from the claim because the quoted sentences say 'stowage bags' and 'such bags'. Limits corrected and extended with caveats from the same section and Section 5.3: the section itself says the acceptability of the ISS and MPCV cargo transfer bags is currently uncertain (p. 29; also p. 14, where HLS testing is reported in which bags propagated fire via burning seams, hook-and-loop fasteners and plastic zippers) and that 'No Nomex material meets flammability requirements for HLS environments containing >36 percent oxygen' (p. 28); and Nomex is flammable in exploration environments containing 36 percent oxygen and above (p. 29). The original limits said 'above 36%' and 'does not meet requirements', now quoted as the source words it.

claim: In its section on stowage bags, JSC 29353D says swollen or otherwise damaged lithium-ion batteries require additional battery-specific containment.
quote: Swollen or otherwise damaged lithium-ion batteries require additional battery-specific containment.
source_title: Flammability Configuration Analysis for Spacecraft Applications, JSC 29353D (December 2024)
source_authors: Michael D. Pedley (prepared by), NASA Johnson Space Center
locator: Section 8.6 Stowage Bags and Lockers, p. 29
limits: Does not define the containment or the swelling criteria. The preceding sentence of the same section says certified, undamaged batteries, including lithium-ion rechargeable batteries, may be stowed inside such bags without additional containment, which is the contrast this sentence draws. It refers to the ISS and MPCV stowage-bag context.
usefulness: (b) Placement rule for the failure state: a swollen or damaged battery must not be stowed like a normal one.
verifier_note: Quote re-checked: found, exact (10 words), Section 8.6, printed p. 29 confirmed. Claim narrowed: 'beyond a standard stowage bag' is read from the preceding sentence (certified, undamaged batteries may go in such bags without additional containment), so the claim now states what the quoted sentence says and cites the context in the limits.
